chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Safwan from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I have made it upon myself two rak'ahs of gratitude to Allah, which I pray during travel and residence. Should I pray them during travel in the day?' He said, 'Yes.' Then he said, 'I dislike compulsion (al-ijab) that a man imposes upon himself.' I said: 'I did not make them obligatory upon me for Allah; rather, I made that upon myself to pray them as gratitude to Allah, and I did not obligate them for Allah upon myself so that I would abandon them if I wished.' He said, 'Yes.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on voluntary gratitude prayers (Shukr) and can they be abandoned?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the legal status of *nadr* (vows) for voluntary prayers, distinguishing between a vow that creates binding obligation (*ijab*) and one that remains a personal commitment of gratitude (*shukr*). He notes that while the companion performed these two rak'ahs in both travel and residence, the Imam cautions against making voluntary acts strictly obligatory upon oneself, as this may lead to neglect if one chooses to abandon them. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that the intent behind a vow determines its legal weight, offering flexibility in supererogatory worship.
